articles.text: The Wildwood Dads’ Club fired up the barbecue on campus last week, welcoming back Piedmont families to the new school year. The dads took over the lower playground to host the fun on Thursday, August 20 as part of a school night event that fed the whole family. The Dads like to have a little fun so they dressed up as hot dogs, mustard and other condiments. Kids rode bikes and played on the playground and blacktop. The Bay Area’s nice August weather helped boost attendance, with many parents coming to let their kids run free at school with their newly reunited friends. The event focused on camaraderie more than fundraising. It let parents catch up with each other about family vacations over the summer and tips on how to get back into the rhythm of the school year. More than a dozen dads volunteered at the event, making sure the burgers and dogs were well distributed and no one went hungry. The club welcomed kindergarten dads to the fold replenishing its roster after graduation from 5th grade turned a group of dads into alumni last May. Up next for the club will be its annual Pumpkin Patch in October, supplying the local region with everything needed for Halloween in one stop at Coaches Field. Wildwood Dads’ Club Officers dressed in BBQ costumes for the Welcome Back Barbecue on August 20. Pictured are Nimesh Singh (left) (Treasurer), Grady Snyder (Officer Emeritus), Alex Danoff (Co-President), Dave Rochwerger (Secretary), Darren Rees (Vice President), and Sergio Serna (Co-President) A Celebration of Life is scheduled for John Morrison on Saturday, September 12, at 2 p.m. in the John Morrison Gymnasium at Piedmont Middle School, 740 Magnolia Avenue. The longtime middle school principal died on August 7, 2026, at the age of 84.

articles.text: Mary was a much-loved member of the church where I serve as the Interim Pastor. She touched many in her long life. Her memorial service was truly a celebration of life. One of the people who eulogized her at that service was her brother-in-law. He spoke warmly of family travels and gatherings. He said that Mary taught him to savor a glass of wine and a leisurely dinner. He said she taught him that “life is more than a hot dog eating contest.” The most famous hot dog eating contest in the world is Nathan’s which takes place on Brooklyn’s Coney Island on the Fourth of July. The men’s record holder is Joey Chestnut who ate 76 hot dogs and buns in ten minutes in 2021. The women’s record holder is Miki Sudo who consumed 51 in 2024. Hot dog eating contests are about speed and conspicuous consumption. It seems that savoring, relaxing, resting and reflecting are not high values at hot dog eating contests. In his instruction to his followers about how best to live their lives Jesus said, “Behold the birds of the air” and “Consider the lilies of the field.” Behold and consider are not hurry words. They are not rush words. They are not consume frantically words. They are not hot dog eating contest words. They are slow down words, take a moment words, cool your jets words. A literary character who comes to mind is Agatha Christie’s somewhat eccentric detective, Hercule Poirot. Poirot is small of stature, large of head and absolutely committed to going slow, considering methodically and taking time to do nothing more than to think, to engage the “little gray cells” of his brain. He often irritates his associates with his refusal to rush around searching for clues and his commitment simply to contemplate. Poirot is not a hot dog eating contest sort of detective. In urging his community to perceive the amazing, complex, diverse and beautiful body that is church, the apostle Paul writes, We have gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: prophecy, in proportion to faith; ministry in ministering; the teacher in teaching; the encourager in encouragement; the giver, in sincerity; the leader in diligence; the compassionate in cheerfulness. We cannot see this amazing grace, this amazing giftedness, without slowing down to behold, without pausing to consider. Acting like we are in a hot dog eating contest is a guarantee that we will miss the profound vision that is our life together. Let us consider. Let us behold. Let us press pause on our hot dog eating contest lives. Instead, let us set our gaze on the goodness of life and so embrace lives that are good. Pastor Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church at Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard in Oakland.

articles.text: As the weather turns hotter and vegetation dries out, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to prepare their yards for fire season by trimming trees and shrubs, clearing flammable materials, and removing dead vegetation around their property. The fire department recommends downloading a checklist for preparing your yard at piedmont. The East Bay hills have experienced multiple significant wildfires in September and October in the last 150 years. Those events and recent wildfires across California have taught us that our communities are best protected when everyone takes steps to manage the vegetation around their homes, which helps to reduce the spread and severity of fires when they start. You can do your part by taking a few simple protective measures in your yard every fall. Make time in the next few weeks to prepare your property: • Clear debris and flammable materials. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your yard. Clear leaves and pine needles from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove flammable materials, such as paint or propane containers, from under decks and away from buildings. • Trim plants of any dead or dying material. It’s important to keep all plants in your yard • • watered and well-maintained. Remove any dead or dying vegetation. If you have trees that shed bark or leaves, such as eucalyptus, remove any shed debris. Create space between plants and your home. Remove branches that hang over your roof or are within 10 feet of your chimney. Prune plants away from buildings. This buffer area will help protect your house and give firefighters space to defend your home during a fire. Trim trees for vertical clearance. articles.text: The best practice in vegetation management is to remove all vegetation within five feet of your home. Even if this is not currently feasible for you, taking protective measures in your yard will increase your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire and reduce risk to our whole community. Use this checklist to prepare your yard. CREATE SPACE Maintaining adequate space between plants, structures, and other objects on your property makes it harder for a fire to spread. Trim trees so that the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground, or 3 times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. Trim trees so that branches are 10 feet apart from other trees. Remove branches within 10 feet of your chimney. Remove branches that hang over your roof. Remove or prune plants and shrubs near windows. Move patio furniture, wood piles, etc. away from plants. CLEAR DEBRIS & FLAMMABLE MATERIAL Clear leaves, pine needles, and other debris from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your property. Remove plant debris and other flammable materials, such as propane containers and paint from under decks. KEEP PLANTS WELL MAINTAINED Whether you have natives or non-natives, the most important thing is to keep all plants in your yard watered and well-maintained. Trim any dead or dying material from plants. Keep plants watered - especially any plants located within five feet of your home. If you have Eucalyptus trees, remove any shedding bark and leaves. Minimum Vertical Clearance: Avoid Fire "Ladders" Lack of vertical space between shrubs and trees allows fire to move from the ground to treetops like a ladder, leading to more intense fires. 3X X Trim trees so the lowest branches are 3 times the height of shrubs below. For example, if a 5 foot shrub is growing near a tree, the lowest branch should be be 15 feet above it - 20 feet from the ground. We're here to help! articles.text: At 12 years old, Cece knows exactly what she wants: quality time with her favorite people, plenty of affection, and your undivided attention. She has mild heart disease that currently requires no medication, diet changes, or exercise restrictions, but she’ll need annual check-ins with a veterinary cardiologist. pages.text: Wednesday, August 26, 2026 5 BUSINESS SPOTLIGHT By Jake Lannon Quality Body & Fender was founded in 1979 by David and Angie Perez. After moving in 1984, they’ve been at their current location at 2510 Martin Luther King Jr. Way for the last 42 years. David Perez was honored by California’s Hispanic Chamber of Commerce for his dedication and services to the Hispanic community as a renowned Latino Quality Body & Fender business owner. Today it is still a family-run business with Jacqueline Perez Kalafate as the GM and Michael Perez assisting Angie. Jacqueline entered the business as a kid, answering phones in the office and washing windows for 10 cents. It was after Jacqueline finished college that she took the business seriously and dedicated time to help out her father. “I believe he started to entice me, telling me he needed some help in the office, and I came to work after finishing college. I had a different career, so I helped in the office one day a week, and that was it. Then he needed two days a week. In 2010, he asked me to come three days a week, and because I had another job, I said, okay, well, let me commit to a year, and I will work full time. And if I like it, I’ll stay on,” said Jacqueline. Jacqueline spent that time Jacqueline Perez with her experienced office staff ATLAS HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY Old Fashioned Service and High-Quality Installations Jacqueline and her mother Angie Perez standing in front of their certifications, showcasing their longstanding reliability. handling contracts and learning to write estimates, eventually becoming an official estimator and manager for the business. Jacqueline would take over the business after her father fell ill and passed away in 2020. Ever since, Jacqueline and her family have carried their father’s legacy and dedication to the community through the business. “My father was born and raised in Oakland, and he was very ingrained in the community at different levels. No one was below him. He respected everyone at the same level, and that showed through with our customers,” Jacqueline continued. “We have people that are struggling, but we help them repair their car just as we would for the CEOs. We understand that everyone’s car is very important to them. We are compassionate enough to know that no one wants to see us. We’re not someone who wants to be visited; it’s stressful and overwhelming. But we have a staff that is trained to be compassionate and empathetic to them, to make this process easier.” According to Jacqueline, it’s this customer-focused approach that differentiates them from other repair shops. Their extensive experience and customer-first approach help people feel their vehicle is in safe hands. “The experience, and the connection we have with our customers and the staff that we employ. We have a person who speaks Chinese and Spanish. We’ve had French in the past, Cantonese, and just being able to service everyone from wherever they come, treating them with the same level of respect is something you don’t get in a lot of places,” said Jacqueline. They are a repair facility for Oakland Honda, Berkeley Honda, Oakland Kia, and Oakland Acura. They do work for Toyota, Volkswagen, and Subaru. They do work on all makes and models of foreign and domestic cars. The shop works with the City of Piedmont to repair its city-owned vehicles and recently started working with the City of Oakland. The business is Platinum Certified, a designation for collision repair professionals who maintain high levels of role-relevant training and complete safe, quality repairs. “We don’t like to deliver a car to a customer unless we are satisfied with it, and we see imperfections in a car that most people don’t. I think when customers know that we do that, they appreciate it a little more because they realize, oh, they care. They’re not just pumping me out and taking my money,” said Jacqueline. The Perez family wants the community to know they are dedicated to helping customers in their lowest moments. “We’re here for you so that we can help you when your kids get into an accident. We are your neighbors, and why not trust your neighbors when you’re dealing with something so important to your daily life? Come down, check us out, and get an estimate. You may not be ready to get it repaired now, but down the line, we are here for you,” she said. Readers can find more information about Quality Body & Fender at their website: www. qualitybf.com. articles.text: The Beach School Dads Club will host its 21st annual Pancake Breakfast this Sunday, August 30. The campus will be turned into a breakfast festival of fun for families starting at 9 a.m. with an army of grills churning out hot cakes with music, games and the Chalk Art Festival also on site. Returning Dads Club President (Padre Grande) Rob Doebelin, pulled out all the stops last year and continues the momentum by bringing out Angelo Moore, founder and frontman of Fishbone to join and possibly serenade the party on saxophone. Music will also be supplied by a DJ. “21st birthdays are a big deal. The Beach Dads Club Pancake Breakfast is officially old enough to party, so we feel some responsibility to act accordingly,” said Doebelin. Last year’s event featured a dunk tank and this year the flyer mentions “water surprises.” In cryptic fashion the flyer encourages prospective attendees to “Bring a towel.” Doebelin confirmed there will be a Fun Zone again and that the Good Eggs Market returns for attendees to take home goodies and groceries after eating their fill of hotcakes. The Beach Padres are offering all teachers, staff and their families to eat for free. The Padres are also encouraging firefighters and police officers to come by and eat free as a small gesture of appreciation. Food for the events is being provided by Piedmont Grocery, Mulberry’s Market, and Village Market. “Every single year, those three local institutions come through for us in a big way, and we’re incredibly grateful for their continued support of the Pancake Breakfast and the Beach community,” said Doebelin. “They’ve become part of the tradition at this point.” The Premium Pancake Toppings Bar will also be fully loaded. “Nutella, whipped cream, chocolate chips, berries, sprinkles and enough sugar to make the rest of Sunday somebody else’s problem,” said Doebelin. The pancakes, bacon, sausage, coffee and fruit salad are worth attendance on their own, but for the organizers, a larger reason compels them. “For more than two decades, dads have been showing up, flipping pancakes, volunteering, doing occasionally ridiculous things for the amusement of children and, somewhere along the way, building friendships of their own,” added Doebelin. The Beach Dads Club will celebrate 21 years of philanthropy, pancakes and community this Sunday, August 30 from 9:00 a.m.-12:30 p.m. at 100 Lake Avenue on the Beach Elementary School campus. articles.text: Nina Schwab graduated from Piedmont High in 2024 as the school’s only diver in its history. She intended to attend Carleton College in Minnesota and in March that year she made history for her college by winning the Division 3 NCAA title in the one-meter dive. She was also the runner up in the three-meter dive in a field of 16 divers. Upon entering her junior year, Schwab transferred to the University of Michigan “It’s definitely been a whirlwind. Being a national champ was super exciting, but I wanted a little more from the sport which is why I transferred to Michigan. I’m very excited about it and also a bit nervous. I’ve been spending the summer training with the team,” Schwab said. It marked her second consecutive year to reach the D3 NCAA Championship. She earned firstteam All-American honors as a freshman, finishing third of 29 in the 1-meter dive with a score of 438.20. You would think Schwab’s success as a diver is indicative of a long career that started in her childhood. But Nina only began diving when she was a junior at Piedmont High. During high school, Schwab decided to switch sports from gymnastics after suffering multiple fractures to her back. Her aunt was a former diver and helped lead Nina to make a decision about her athletic career. Looking back to her junior year in high school, becoming a Nina Schwab, PHS Class of 2024, won the Division 3 NCAA Championship in the one-meter dive with Carleton College in March. national champion may have not been on her radar. “I really didn’t have a lot of expectations going into a new sport. My coach said it was possible, but I really didn’t expect to do it in college at all. I was injured all the time and lost my love for gymnastics. My aunt, who dove for the University of Minnesota, recommended the sport, so I just thought I’d try it out. And now here we are,” Schwab said. In 2024 as a high school senior, she finished fourth of 16 divers at the North Coast championships and 16th of 28 in State Championship. Just two years later, she became the best diver in her collegiate division and is now Nina Schwab reached two D3 NCAA Championships at Carleton College.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team’s season got off to a scorching start on Monday, August 24. Playing on the road at American High in Fremont, the Highlanders demolished the Eagles in a one-sided 18-7 win. The PHS offense was humming with a 12-3 lead by halftime while forcing several turnovers mid-pool and launching successful counter attacks one after another. “Our defense was focusing on a press in the lane, and we did a good job of that in the first half,” said coach Rik Krumins. “In the second half, we got into our position and then kind of relaxed. We want to continue being ball hawks. I was impressed with the boys. We got out on the counter, and got into the right areas.” Despite the win, Piedmont went down a man 13 times on the day, including conceding four 5-meter penalty attempts. “I’m not comfortable with the amount of penalties. We want to make sure we’re not in a bad spot so the referees make a call easily,” Krumins said. Still, the PHS defense was stout, including sophomore goalie Dylan Jerez who made 12 saves. “Dylan is one of the most consistent players on the team. He holds us down on defense and we can always rely on him. He’s a great leader in terms of communication,” junior Rylan Patty said of his teammate. Jerez was pinpointed by threeyear starting goalie and Class of 2026 graduate, Luke McAuliffe. “He played summer polo at CCU. At our end-of-season banquet, Luke said, ‘Dylan is the next guy.’ Luke kind of trained him last season so he’s ready to go,” junior Henry Stein added. The Highlanders are off for a week before visiting Newark Memorial on Tuesday, September 1, but look toward a monumental Thursday, September 3 when hosting their first match in Piedmont since 2019. Piedmont’s players were in elementary school the last time PHS hosted a game. Staff Photos Henry Stein had five goals, five assists, and four steals in Piedmont’s season-opener. “I had some great memories at the old Piedmont Pool. Now, the big thing I’ve been noticing is that we’re all so happy to be at the new pool. I don’t want to take it for granted, and want to put as many hours as I can in the pool,” Patty said. “Hopefully the crowd shows up and I see all my friends come to the game to support us. It’s going to be great,” Stein added. Match Recap Piedmont led 6-0 through the first quarter and 12-3 by halftime. They scored five more in the third quarter to go up 17-4, finishing with one goal in the fourth quarter and conceded three. In the first quarter, PHS had three goals by Stein, two goals by Henry Van Den Bos, and one by Patty to hold a commanding 6-0 advantage. Ven Den Bos scored again early in the second quarter before American got its first goal at the 5:43 mark. From there, PHS went on a four-goal scoring run to lead 11-1 with 2:44 left. Stein assisted Van Den Bos, Patty added another, Stein assisted Raffi Banin, and Colin Amen assisted Stein. Later on, Jack Dahling assisted Graham Smith to make it 12-2 with 1:27 left. PHS scored another four straight goals in the third by way of Stein assisting Walker Wilson, Stein assisting Patty, Van Den Bos assisting Stein, and Stein assisting Van Den Bos. Leo Maltz got Piedmont’s 17th goal following a steal and breakaway. Dahling scored Piedmont’s final goal with 2:06 left in the fourth quarter by way of a five-meter penalty shot. Final stats: Stein scored five goals, five assists, and four steals. Van Den Bos had five goals and two steals. Patty had three goals and two steals. Banin had one goal, one assist, and four steals. Wilson, Dahling and Smith had one goal and steal. Amen had one assist and steal. Jerez had 12 saves. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0 overall) visits Newark Memorial on Tuesday, September 1 at 5:30 p.m. They also host James Logan in Piedmont on Thursday, September 3 at the same time. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team is off to a strong start to the season. After opening their campaign with a close 3-2 loss to Berean Christian at home on Thursday, August 20, they followed up by going undefeated (4-0) at the Stockton Classic hosted by Edison HS to win their bracket on Saturday, August 22. At Stockton, they closed with a 25-20, 25-20 win over Manteca in the finals. In their second match against Lathrop, they lost the first set 25-13 before responding with 25-7, 15-9 wins to close. In the semifinals against Edison, they similarly lost the first set 25-14 but bounced back with 25-11, 15-8 wins. “Overall, we really showed a lot of growth. It’s great to win, but the team really got better over the weekend. Against Lathrop, we got beat badly in the first set… but we showed resilience and adjusted to the pressure,” said co-head coach Mike Glass. “Edison was another case where we saw a lot of growth on the team with defensive adjustments. Our strong play against Edison carried into Manteca where we didn’t have any service errors the entire game.” Maika Ting was instrumental offensively throughout the tournament with 16 total kills in four matches. Piedmont’s service game was strong, including libero Allyson Huynh with 14 aces. Mia Bechtel finished the final match over Manteca with an ace. “Maika had 16 kills and only two hitting errors. Allyson was our ace leader with 14 aces and only a single serving error. In our final match against Manteca we had no serve receive errors,” co-head coach Jason Mongue added. The tournament success was a nice rebound after the season-opening loss to Berean Christian. PHS dominated the first set 25-13, and held leads in the second, third, and fifth sets before dropping each. “We’ve only had two weeks of practice, and there are a lot of new players on this team. It’ll take some adjusting, but I’m confident our success will come quickly and we’ll bond really fast,” Huynh said following the match. 2-0 over Manteca In the first set, both teams traded points with Manteca holding an early 5-3 lead. From there, Piedmont eventually took the lead by scoring six of seven points to go up 9-6 with two kills by Bailey, one by Maika Ting, and a block by Sofia Meyer. Holding a 14-11 lead, PHS rallied another six of seven points to extend the gap to 20-12 with another two kills by Bailey and one by Lucia Dorsey. Near the end of the set, Manteca scored three straight to cut the deficit to 24-20, but Bailey finished the set with a winning spike. It was a similar start to the second set with Manteca taking an 8-7 lead. PHS regained the lead at 9-8 with an ace by Mia Bechtel and never relinquished. At 13-11, the Highlanders scored six straight points to go up 19-11 with kills by Dorsey, Bailey, and an ace by Carina Vora. With a 23-16 lead, Manteca scored four straight to cut Piedmont’s lead to 23-20. From there, PHS scored via a service error and finished the tournament with an ace by Bechtel. 2-1 over Edison Piedmont defeated the hosting school in three sets by scores of 14-25, 25-11, 15-8. articles.text: PEF Board Members (top row): Mark McLaughlin, Billy Deitch, Dan Saper, Rick Raushenbush, Michael Gross and Matt Olson; (middle row): Marco Gonzalez-Navarro, Sarah Pearson, Nellie Thornton, Zeena Fakery, Jennie Stomberg, Molly Lloyd, Julia Ruthven; (bottom row): Heather Frank, Adam Fishman, Kim Hunter, Rita Fabi, and Board Chair, Bridget Schreiber The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) is kicking off the 2026-27 school year with renewed energy and an ambitious commitment to supporting Piedmont’s students, teachers and schools. On Wednesday, August 19, PEF’s Board of Directors held its first meeting of the school year and welcomed new board members Billy Deitch, Mark McLaughlin and Nellie Thornton. The board also launched its committee work for the year and began planning the programs, fundraising efforts and community initiatives that will support Piedmont schools throughout the 2026-27 academic year. A highlight of the meeting was the announcement that PEF will present Piedmont Unified School District with a record-breaking $4,355,000 funding check at the September 9 meeting of the Piedmont Unified School District Board of Education. The funding represents the extraordinary generosity of the Piedmont community and PEF’s ongoing commitment to providing resources that enhance the educational experience for every student. “We are incredibly excited about the year ahead,” said PEF Executive Director Heather Frank. “Our community continues to demonstrate that when we come together to support our schools, we can make a meaningful difference for every student. This year’s record funding is a tremendous accomplishment and a reminder of what is possible when our entire community steps up.” PEF also announced that its annual Giving Campaign will launch Tuesday, September 22. The Giving Campaign is PEF’s largest fundraising effort of the year and plays a critical role in bridging the gap between the funding PUSD receives from state and local sources and the actual cost of providing the high-quality education Piedmont families value. The campaign will be led this year by co-chairs Bindu Lokre, Brook Meakins and Ellie Somers, who are focused on bringing the entire community together in support of Piedmont schools. “Schools are the heart of our community, and the community supports the schools,” said Lokre, Meakins and Somers. “We are excited to energize our community and get as many people as possible involved in this essential effort.” PEF is also working alongside the Parents’ Clubs and school support groups to help launch a new year of programs and opportunities for students and families. This includes Parents’ Club membership campaigns at each school and a variety of events and fundraisers throughout the year. Families can learn more about Parents’ Club memberships, student programs, upcoming events and other ways to support Piedmont schools at PiedmontStore. org. As the new school year begins, PEF is looking forward to another year of partnership, generosity and community support, and to working toward its vision of ensuring that Piedmont’s schools have the resources they need to provide an exceptional education for every student. About PEF Piedmont Education Foundation is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization whose mission is to provide sustained financial support to Piedmont schools through fundraising and community engagement. Led by a volunteer board of directors, Piedmont Education Foundation manages annual fundraising campaigns, hosts events, and acts as a fiscal sponsor for multiple Piedmont school support organizations. articles.text: and Ariel Rodriguez The school year is starting again, and this time of transition can feel both exciting and overwhelming. As we enter the new school year, we have the unique opportunity to make a fresh start: new classes, new teachers, and, perhaps, a new perspective. Here are some steps to help you start the school year feeling empowered. Step 1 – Reflect For many of us, the start of the school year can feel like a mad scramble, but setting aside even a few minutes to reflect on the previous school year can make a meaningful difference. Ask yourself, “What worked well last school year and how did that make me feel?” Then, ask yourself, “What was challenging last school year and how did that make me feel?” Write down a few responses for each question. Keep your responses brief, but try to be specific. Here are some examples: • “having a separate binder for each class helped me feel organized” • “we usually run late on Monday mornings which makes me feel anxious” Step 2 – Plan If something is working for you, don’t change it! Acknowledge how helpful it’s been and re-commit to that behavior going forward. Once you identify a challenge, acknowledge that it exists and work to make changes. If Monday mornings feel frantic and stressful in your household, write down some ideas for how you might be able to change that: • “pick out Monday’s outfit on Sunday” • “pack my backpack on Sunday evening” • “do homework on Saturday and Sunday so that I don’t have to stay up late on Sunday night to finish everything” After you’ve made your list of ideas, pick one or two to try. Step 3 – Check in For the last month, you’ve used Sunday to pick Monday’s outfit and to pack your backpack. Do you feel less stressed? Are you making it to school on time? If the answer is yes — congratulations! You’ve found a behavior that helps you overcome a challenge. Keep doing what you’re doing. If the answer is no, that’s OK. Go back to your list and try another idea from your brainstorm until you find something that does work for you. Feeling Empowered in the New School Year By Emily Thompson and Ariel Rodriguez The school year is starting again, and this time of transition can feel both exciting and overwhelming. As we enter the new school year, we have the unique opportunity to make a fresh start: new classes, new teachers, and, perhaps, a new perspective. Here are some steps to help you start the school year feeling empowered. Step 1 – Reflect For many of us, the start of the school year can feel like a mad scramble, but setting aside even a few minutes to reflect on the previous school year can make a meaningful difference. Ask yourself, “What worked well last school year and how did that make me feel?” Then, ask yourself, “What was challenging last school year and how did that make me feel?” Write down a few responses for each question. Keep your responses brief, but try to be specific. Here are some examples: • “having a separate binder for each class helped me feel organized” • “we usually run late on Monday mornings which makes me feel anxious” Step 2 – Plan If something is working for you, don’t change it! Acknowledge how helpful it’s been and re-commit to that behavior going forward. Once you identify a challenge, acknowledge that it exists and work to make changes. If Monday mornings feel frantic and stressful in your household, write down some ideas for how you might be able to change that: • “pick out Monday’s outfit on Sunday” • “pack my backpack on Sunday evening” • “do homework on Saturday and Sunday so that I don’t have to stay up late on Sunday night to finish everything” After you’ve made your list of ideas, pick one or two to try. Step 3 – Check in For the last month, you’ve used Sunday to pick Monday’s outfit and to pack your backpack. Do you feel less stressed? Are you making it to school on time? If the answer is yes — congratulations! You’ve found a behavior that helps you overcome a challenge. Keep doing what you’re doing. If the answer is no, that’s OK. Go back to your list and try another idea from your brainstorm until you find something that does work for you. This process of checking in with yourself is especially helpful during times of transition and can help you feel empowered to grow not only as a student but as a person! articles.text: Folks attend a guided tour through the redwoods that surround Chabot as they learn about the land and its history. Redwood Regional Park, which surrounds Chabot Space & Science Center, is abundant in beautiful plant and animal life. A visit to Chabot offers the opportunity to learn about the wonders of our galaxy and the fascinating ecosystem of the planet we call home. Surrounding Chabot is a stunning and lush landscape filled with many types of animals, plants, and geology. One of the most famous plants in the area are the coast redwoods. These magnificent giants and the land that they sit on remind us of the rich history in the East Bay and that science is actively around us. A Giant’s History There was once a time when redwood trees were found across North America. In the past, the redwoods of the East Bay once reached from the Oakland Hills to Moraga. A group of especially tall redwoods, dubbed the Navigation Trees, acted as landmarks that helped safely guide ships through the San Francisco Bay. Unfortunately, due to a combination of changing climates and an increase in housing during the 1800s, a significant number of redwoods in the East Bay no longer exist. However, the descendants of these incredible ancient giants can be found predominantly in the Redwood Regional Park that surrounds Chabot. Redwood Regional Park encompasses the grounds of Chabot and is one of the many beautiful parks in the East Bay Regional Park District. The land within these parks is the ancestral home to a diverse group of indigenous people who are descended from Ohlone, Bay Miwok, and Delta Yokuts ancestral tribes. Members of the groups held an in-depth knowledge of the plants and animals in the areas where they lived. The vast knowledge of these groups fueled their ability to expertly manage the land in ways that would benefit and enhance all living things in the area. Today, the descendants of these groups are actively involved in the preservation and restoration of their ancestral lands. The Science of Redwoods Coast redwoods belong to the cypress family and are the tallest trees in the world. Hyperion, a coast redwood in Humboldt County, California, stands at 380 feet high, making it the tallest tree known in the world! To put that into perspective, the planetarium dome here at Chabot is 70 feet high. Even if we were to stack five planetarium domes on top of each other, it still would not quite reach the height of the tallest coast redwood. Coast redwoods are evergreen plants, which means their foliage stays green and functional year-round. The thick and resistant bark of coast redwoods has given these exquisite giants the ability to withstand fire. These beautiful giants are also conifers, which means they produce cones and needles. Despite their unusual appearance, the needles of redwoods are technically their leaves. Redwood needles are flat and pointed on both ends, providing the critical function of photosynthesis. Experience the History & Science Firsthand Experience an unforgettable evening of nature, history, and stargazing with our Hike & Sip series, a program designed for adults 21 and over. On Saturday, August 29th, explore the majestic Redwood forest, guided by Chabot’s knowledgeable outdoor educators, and learn about the ecosystem, the cultural heritage of the Ohlone peoples, and Oakland’s rich history. After your hike, unwind on Chabot’s Observation Deck with drinks and charcuterie. End the night with stargazing through telescopes (weather permitting) and star stories brought to life under the night skies. Visit chabotspace. org for more information on this incredible experience!

articles.text: Alicia Mason stars as Effie in Shotgun Players’ Iphigenia in Splott. Shotgun Players has extended its production of Iphigenia in Splott, Gary Owen’s one-person play inspired by Euripides’ Iphigenia in Aulis, through Saturday, August 29. Directed by Michelle Talgarow, the production marks the company’s first one-person performance and follows Effie, a modern-day version of Iphigenia who lives in the working-class town of Splott in Wales. Effie stumbles through life before facing a choice between selfless sacrifice and the welfare of her community. The production explores the socioeconomic conditions of the working class through Effie’s experience of systemic failure, Talgarow said. “Don’t let the title fool you, this isn’t just a retelling of the ancient Greek myth,” she added. “It is a sharp, modern thrill ride set in working-class Wales. It’s just one actor on stage for 75 minutes, and she will absolutely blow you away with her energy, wit, wry humor, and a story that feels incredibly urgent right now.” Alicia Mason stars as Effie. Talgarow returns to Shotgun Players after directing the company’s 2024 production of Thirty-Six. The production follows the release of Effi o Blaenau, a Welsh-language film adaptation that premiered at the Glasgow Film Festival in March of this year and received a full U.K. theatrical release in June. Tickets are available for purchase at www.shotgunplayers. org/show/iphegenia/ or by calling the box office at 510-841-6500.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre opens its 2026-27 season with Eduardo Machado’s The Cook, running September 4 through October 11. Directed by Berkeley Rep Associate Artistic Director David Mendizábal, the play follows an aristocratic Cuban family that flees Havana for Miami on the eve of Fidel Castro’s revolution. The family leaves its mansion in the care of Gladys, their cook, who promises to protect the home until they return. articles.text: Finding happiness isn’t so difficult. All you need to know is where to go. Perhaps this sounds simplistic and perhaps it is. I suggest that it is best to sidestep the news media in general. They are very good at acknowledging the kamikaze ardor for the bad. Fortunately, the Piedmont Post is a rare exception. I suggest that happiness is certainly not contemplating the misery of another. Some people and some organizations know this. One of them is the Musicians’ Union. Every year, they host a “thank you luncheon” for lifetime members of the union. For many years the rendezvous was at Nick’s Rockaway Beach restaurant. It is interesting to note that Nick’s is celebrating 99 years of successful dining pleasure. That’s rather a long time to enjoy success. Please note that quite a few of the musicians are of a very advanced age. If I heard correctly, the oldest musician in attendance was also 99 years old. The day began with a very pleasant drive to Pacifica. Then we saw lots of friends. A band had been engaged to entertain us and they played nonstop. After about an hour, we sat down to enjoy lunch. Dining has been described as eating good food in good company and that’s the way it was on Monday. Nick’s is a very pleasant restaurant and they serve excellent food abetted by excellent service. Portions are very large. The union picked up the tab so I cannot tell you about the price but I think that it was very reasonable. Everyone in attendance was offered the choice of chicken, fish, or prime rib. Debbie and I chose one fish and one prime rib. Take a look at the accompanying photograph of the prime rib. It was just about the best I have ever had, and it overflowed the plate. Kudos to Nick’s and kudos to the Musicians’ Union for knowing how to show appreciation. Finding happiness can be a simple equation. When you enjoy music with good friends and good food you have found one version of happiness. Bring those three things together and you have a very good recipe. This glorious prime rib is an example of the food at Nick‘s Rockaway Beach restaurant. It was delicious and so big that Samson could’ve used it in battle.

articles.text: An exhibition featuring Henri Matisse’s Femme au chapeau, a painting widely regarded as a landmark of modern art, leaves the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on SepThe exhibition, titled Matisse’s Femme au chapeau: A Modern Scandal, opened May 16 and examines the history, reception and lasting influence of the 1905 portrait, which is part of SFMOMA’s permanent collection. The painting debuted at the Salon d’Automne in Paris in 1905 and became associated with Fauvism, the first French avantgarde art movement of the 20th century. The exhibition explores the work’s historical context, subject, provenance and circulation through exhibitions and publications, while also considering its impact on later generations of artists. “We are thrilled to have this opportunity to share the full story of Matisse’s Femme au chapeau—a painting that is emblematic of the artist’s radical break from convention in the early years of his career,” Janet Bishop, SFMOMA Chief Curator, said in a press release. “Arguably SFMOMA’s most art-historically significant work of art, Femme au chapeau began sending shockwaves through the art world as soon as it left Matisse’s studio and has captivated viewers ever since,” Bishop added. The exhibition also traces the painting’s ownership history. American collectors Leo and Gertrude Stein acquired the work in 1905 while living in Paris. It later entered the collection of Michael and Sarah Stein, who brought it to the Bay Area in 1935. The painting was first exhibited in the United States at the San Francisco Museum of Art, now SFMOMA, in 1936. It entered the museum’s collection in 1991 through a bequest from Elise S. Haas. “Par t of our vision at SFMOMA is to encourage our visitors to see the world— and art—in new ways,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “With stunning paintings by Matisse and his peers, as well as work by some of the most exceptional artists working today, this exhibition promises to captivate SFMOMA visitors.” Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/ for more information. articles.text: Piedmont Roundup Market Observations, Insider Wisdom & The Week in Piedmont Real Estate As students head back to class, the City has quietly rewritten the Civic Center’s traffic choreography. Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland Avenues is now one-way northbound toward Oakland, drivers can no longer turn onto Bonita from Oakland, and the Havens Elementary drop-off zone that used to live on Bonita has been eliminated. If you’re a Havens family, the main show has moved to Highland Avenue, where loading zones now line both sides of the street and a crossing guard helps the littlest Piedmonters across. The changes hit Havens families hardest but ripple through every route to the other schools and facilities in the Civic Center. Review your usual drive before the first bell and allow extra time in week one, because the first week of a new traffic pattern is always chaos wearing a polite smile. The Piedmont Police Department will station staff at the Bonita/Oakland intersection during that first week to assist with the transition, which is cityspeak for “we know this is going to be a mess, please be patient.” In the News: Pool Parking Pushback June of this year, from very smart young journalists at The Highlander comes a well-put-together parking pushback. When will municipal government learn that revolutions are built on inconvenienced citizens? Piedmont’s pool parking, which is near Piedmont’s schools, is already drawing pushback from students, and the complaints are not hard to understand. The city converted 30 spaces to two-hour parking and stepped-up enforcement, which means fewer longterm spots for PHS, MHS, and PMS students and staff. The Highlander editorial argues the result will be more tardies, more tickets, and more frustration for teachers who already deal with limited parking. It also notes that the new pool does not justify making weekday school parking worse, especially when swim and water polo practices themselves run about two hours. The bigger issue is process. Students say many only learned about the changes after getting ticketed, and a student petition to reverse the decision quickly gathered hundreds of signatures. If you want people to support civic change, start by not making their daily lives harder. I wanted to chalk it up to them being busy but then I realized none of the ones I visited get the Post delivered to their homes. I did meet some of the residents on that tour and got some suggestions about how to make this a better column. I am listening. The best suggestion was to add a list of all addresses that changed hands for the month, akin to a police blotter. I’ll make sure to add all the ones that actually make the Multiple Listing Service (MLS). My favorite thing heard on tour came from a resident, wearing orange Crocs, who was very excited about the view of the lake from one of the properties on tour. Children have a way of cutting through the sales pitch to the important things. Did You Know Piedmont, yes, this Piedmont, has a lake. Most of us know the local landmarks, but there’s a secret hidden right behind the homes on Sotelo Avenue: Tyson Lake. Originally created in the early 20th century by George H. Tyson, who dammed a small local creek to build a private swimming hole, it remains one of the city’s bestkept secrets. Today, the lake is strictly private — managed by a neighborhood association rather than the city — and serves as a scenic (some say haunted) retreat for the surrounding homeowners. It’s a staple of local lore and often highlighted during Walking Piedmont tours, but don’t go looking for a public entrance; there isn’t one. pages.text: 26 26 Wednesday, August 26, 2026 I’ve called the Bay Area home since 2007, when I moved here from Sacramento to be closer to my then-boyfriend, now husband. I may be a transplant, but our family’s roots in the Bay run deep. My husband’s mother was born in San Francisco and attended Bay Area schools, and his grandfather, Sam Johnstone, founded NorCal Supply in 1950, a family business my husband continues to run today. Grandpa Sam was also a USF Hall of Famer who believed deeply in giving back to the community and his alma mater. That tradition is something we’re proud to continue with our own family. Today, we’re raising three boys who attend Crocker Highlands schools and The Renaissance International School. I’m a proud Platinum Sponsor of my kids’ soccer club and believe that being part of a community means showing up for it, not just living in it. That philosophy carries into my real estate business, too. My selling style may be a little unconventional, and I like it that way. When I returned to real estate full-time, longtime Piedmont residents Steve and Corki Recht gave me a twoweek listing opportunity to sell their home at 83 Hazel Lane. Rather than disrupting their lives with months of preparation, staging and open houses, I took a quiet, highly targeted approach. We sold the home off-market for $5.5 million, all cash, with no staging and no open house. Corki had plenty of friends deeply rooted in Piedmont real estate, but she saw something in me and gave this gal an opportunity. I’m incredibly proud that I exceeded her expectations. In 1974, the city designated four official off-leash zones: Blair Park and portions of Dracena and Linda parks. Rather than building traditional fenced enclosures, Piedmont selected natural areas already favored by dog owners— wooded spots with trails and minimal interference with athletic fields. Fences were added to Linda Park in the 1990s, though environmental and water-quality issues forced its closure in 2025. Following habitat restoration, Linda Park reopened as an on-leash space. To balance freedom with responsibility, Piedmont added an off-leash permit system in 2000, requiring dog owners to purchase a permit and show proof of licensing and vaccinations. Sean noted that doing his research revealed a sweet local reality: some dog-walking groups have included the same neighbors for decades. The parks aren’t just thoroughfares; they are community hubs. Walking dogs echoes the spirit of Walking on Wednesdays—getting outside, moving together and building connections. After thanking Sean for the lively tour, the group looped along Dracena, Blair, Hillside and Bonita avenues, returning to Exedra Plaza refreshed and inspired. pages.text: Wednesday, August 26, 2026 31 By Michael Gross When I ask my kids what they love about Cub Scouts, the answer is simple: spending time outside with friends and visiting beautiful places. They love camping — Mt. Diablo is a favorite spot — and biking on the Bay Trail. They especially enjoy learning skills that feel a little dangerous, like using knives, building campfires, cooking, and archery. When my children camp under the trees and stars, a wonderful shift occurs: screens disappear from their thoughts. When children are given a compelling outdoor environment, they’re too busy having fun engaging with nature. This is true for both my fourth-grade daughter and my seventh-grade son, who has since moved on to Scouts. Following in her brother’s footsteps, my daughter, already busy with swimming and ballet, fell in love with Cubs in her own right. Cub Scouts gives children the opportunity to discover that they are capable of more than they realize.
